text: collisions in multiple dimensions. It is more common for collisions to occur in 2D, where the initial velocity vectors can be decomposed into components. Recall that momentum is related to force through the relation vector f equals d vector p over dt. Therefore, both the momentum and force can be written in their component forms together as f sub x equals dp sub x over dt. f sub y equals dp sub y over dt. f sub z equals dp sub z over dt. Remember, these equations are Newton's second law in vector and component form. Since Newton's second law is true in each direction individually, it follows that conservation of momentum is true in each direction independently, the Newton's third law. We can now write down the expression for conservation of momentum following the same procedure, that is, decompose it into components. p sub x final equals p sub 1x initial plus p sub 2x initial. p sub y final equals p sub 1y initial plus p sub 2. y initial. Below shows the procedure graphically, where the two initial momenta vector p sub 1 initial and vector p sub 2 initial come into the collision point, gray dot at the origin and the final combined momentum vector p sub f exits after the collision. Checkpoint, pause and check your understanding. In a two-dimensional collision, why do you need one momentum equation for each component direction? We solve each of the two component equations independently to obtain the x and y components for the final momentum's velocity vector. Here is an example for the x components. p sub x final equals p sub 1x initial plus p sub 2x initial. m v sub x final equals m sub 1 v sub 1x initial plus m sub 2 v sub 2x initial. v sub x final equals m sub 1 over m v sub 1x initial plus m sub 2 over m v sub 2x initial, where m represents the total mass of the system. m equals m sub 1 plus m sub 2. Similarly, we can find a y component of the final velocity vector as v sub y final equals m sub 1 over m v sub 1 y initial plus m sub 2 over m v sub 2 y initial. We can combine the components using the Pythagorean theorem to get v final equals magnitude of vector v final equals square root of v sub x final squared plus v sub y final squared. What does this mean physically? This example models a perfectly inelastic collision where the two incoming masses stick together. The component final velocities represent a linear combination of the component initial velocities. Each initial component velocity is scaled by the respective mass divided by the total mass. What happens if m sub 1 is much greater than m sub 2? Let's assume that m sub 1 equals 999 kilograms and m sub 2 equals 1 kilogram. Then we have v sub x final equals 999 over 999 plus 1 v sub 1 x initial plus 1 over 999 plus 1 v sub 2 x initial equals 0.999 v sub 1 x initial plus 0.001 v sub 2 x initial. v sub y final equals 999 over 999 plus 1 v sub 1 y initial plus 1 over 999 plus 1 v sub 2 y initial equals 0.999 v sub 1 y initial plus 0.001 v sub 2 y initial. If v sub 1 initial is greater than v sub 2 initial, the m sub 1 component dominates and the final velocity is more similar to vector v sub 1 initial. If v sub 1 initial is less than v sub 2 initial, the m sub 2 component can still be significant and the final velocity is more similar to vector v sub 2 initial. Think of a bullet hitting an apple. Problem solving strategy. Conservation of momentum in 2D. The method for solving a 2D or even 3D conservation of momentum problem is generally the same as the method for solving a 1D problem, except that you have to conserve momentum in each direction simultaneously. First, identify a closed system. Second, write down the equation that represents the conservation of momentum in each direction and solve it for the desired quantity for the respective direction. Third, if you are calculating a vector quantity, use the Pythagorean theorem to calculate its magnitude. Example problem. Traffic collision. The problem. A small car of mass 1200 kilograms traveling east at 60 kilometers per hour collides with a truck of mass 3000 kilograms traveling north at 40 kilometers per hour. The vehicles lock together after the collision. What is the velocity of the combined wreckage immediately after impact? The worked solution follows. The model. We define the system to be the car plus truck during the brief collision interval. The interaction time is extremely short, so we neglect external impulses such as friction with the road during that instant. Linear momentum of the two vehicle system is therefore conserved during the collision. Because the vehicles lock together and move as a single object after impact, the collision is perfectly in elastic. Kinetic energy is not conserved, but momentum is conserved. We define the plus x direction to point east and the plus y direction to point north. The initial momenta are perpendicular, so momentum conservation must be applied separately in the x and y directions. The math. Let m sub c equals 1200 kilograms and m sub t equals 3000 kilograms. We convert speeds to SI units. 60 kilometers per hour equals 16.7 meters per second and 40 kilometers per hour equals 11.1 meters per second. Conservation of momentum requires vector p final equals vector p initial. The initial momenta components are p sub x initial equals m sub c v sub c and p sub y initial equals m sub t v sub t. After the collision, the combined mass m sub c plus m sub t moves with velocity components v sub x final and v sub y final. Therefore m sub c v sub c equals m sub c plus m sub t times v sub x final. m sub t v sub t equals m sub c plus m sub t times v sub y final. Solving each equation for the velocity components gives v sub x final equals m sub c over m sub c plus m sub t v sub c. v sub y final equals m sub t over m sub c plus m sub t v sub t. Using the given masses, we find v sub x final equals 1200 over 4,200 times 16.7 equals 4.77 meters per second. v sub y final equals 3000 over 4,200 times 11.1 equals 7.93 meters per second. The magnitude of the wreckage velocity is found from the Pythagorean theorem. Vector v final magnitude equals square root of 4.77 squared plus 7.93 squared equals 9.26 meters per second. The direction measured counterclockwise from the plus x axis is theta equals tan to the power of negative 1 of v sub y final over v sub x final equals tan to the power of negative 1 of 7.93 over 4.77 equals 59 degrees. The conclusion immediately after the collision, the wreckage moves with speed vector v final magnitude equals 9.3 meters per second at an angle of 59 degrees north of east. The heavier truck contributes more to the y component of momentum, so the combined motion is tilted strongly northward. Even though the car's speed was larger, its smaller mass means its momentum contribution is smaller than the trucks. Example problem, exploding scuba tank. The problem, a common scuba tank is an aluminum cylinder that weighs 31.7 pounds empty. When full of compressed air, the internal pressure is between 2500 and 3000 psi. Suppose such a tank, which had been sitting motionless, suddenly explodes into three pieces. The first piece, weighing 10 pounds, shoots off horizontally at 235 miles per hour. The second piece, 7 pounds, shoots off at 172 miles per hour, also in the horizontal plane, but at a 19 degrees angle to the first piece. What is the mass and initial velocity of the third piece? Do all work and express your final answer in SI units. The worked solution follows. The model. The system is the scuba tank during the brief explosion. The tank is initially at rest, so the initial momentum of the system is zero. The explosion happens over a very short time, so external impulses, such as gravity, are negligible during that instant, and the tank can be treated as a closed system for momentum. The motion is confined to the horizontal plane, so we choose axes in that plane and apply conservation of momentum in components. We define the plus x direction to be the direction of piece 1's motion, and we take piece 2 to move at an angle 19 degrees above the plus x axis. The math. Conservation of momentum for the explosion gives vector p initial equals vector p final. Because the tank starts from rest, vector p initial equals vector 0, and therefore vector p sub 1 plus vector p sub 2 plus vector p sub 3 equals vector 0. The total mass of the tank is 31.7 pounds, and the three fragments have weights 10 pounds, 7 pounds, and the remainder. Converting to SI units using 1 pound equals 0.4536 kilograms, gives m sub total equals 14.4 kilograms, m sub 1 equals 4.5 kilograms, and m sub 2 equals 3.2 kilograms. So the third mass is m sub 3 equals m sub total minus m sub 1 plus m sub 2 equals 6.7 kilograms. The given speeds are converted using 1 mile per hour equals 0.4470 meters per second, which gives v sub 1 equals 105 meters per second, and v sub 2 equals 77 meters per second. With the plus x axis along piece 1, the momenta of pieces 1 and 2 are vector p sub 1 equals m sub 1 v sub 1 i hat vector p sub 2 equals m sub 2 v sub 2 cosine theta i hat plus m sub 2 v sub 2 sine theta j hat, where theta equals 19 degrees. The third piece must carry the opposite momentum vector p sub 3 equals minus vector p sub 1 plus vector p sub 2. So its components are p sub 3 x equals minus m sub 1 v sub 1 plus m sub 2 v sub 2 cosine theta, and p sub 3 y equals minus m sub 2 v sub 2 sine theta. Evaluating these gives p sub 3 x is approximately equal to minus 710 kilogram meters per second, and p sub 3 y is approximately equal to minus 80 kilogram meters per second. The momentum magnitude is vector p sub 3 equals square root of p sub 3 x to the power of 2 plus p sub 3 y to the power of 2 is approximately equal to 710 kilogram meters per second. So the speed of the third piece is v sub 3 equals vector p sub 3 over m sub 3 is approximately equal to 710 over 6.7 meters per second equals 110 meters per second. The direction of vector v sub 3 is the same as the direction of vector p sub 3. The angle below the negative x-axis is set by 10 phi equals p sub 3 y over p sub 3 x, which gives phi is approximately equal to 6.4 degrees. This means the third piece travels mostly opposite piece 1, deflected slightly toward negative y. The conclusion, the third fragment has mass m sub 3 equals 6.7 kilograms, and initial speed v sub 3 equals 110 meters per second. Its velocity points approximately 6.4 degrees below the negative x direction. Equivalently about 6.4 degrees south of west if plus x is east.
